ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure there is a pentagon, with vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E in clockwise/surrounding order. The side lengths marked on the figure are AB=16, BC=14, CD=17, DE=13, EA=14. The problem statement says to draw circles with A, B, C, D, E as centers respectively, and the two circles corresponding to the two ends of each side are tangent. Reasoning: Let the radii of the circles with A, B, C, D, E as centers be a, b, c, d, e respectively. Since the circles at the two ends of each side are tangent, the sum of the corresponding two radii equals that side length: a+b=16, b+c=14, c+d=17, d+e=13, e+a=14. From a+b=16, get b=16-a; from b+c=14, get c=14-b=a-2; from c+d=17, get d=17-c=19-a; from d+e=13, get e=13-d=a-6. Substitute into e+a=14, get (a-6)+a=14, that is 2a=20, so a=10. Thus b=6, c=8, d=9, e=4. The largest radius is a=10, therefore the center of the largest circle is A.

method.method_draft: Read the pentagon vertices in cyclic order from the image as A-B-C-D-E, with side lengths AB=16, BC=14, CD=17, DE=13, and EA=14. Let the radii of the circles centered at A, B, C, D, E be a, b, c, d, e. From the text, circles at the two ends of every side touch, so each side length equals the sum of the two corresponding radii: a+b=16, b+c=14, c+d=17, d+e=13, e+a=14. Substitute around the cycle: b=16-a, c=a-2, d=19-a, e=a-6. Use e+a=14 to get 2a-6=14, so a=10. Then b=6, c=8, d=9, e=4, so the biggest circle is centered at A.
